## Exercise 2.1: Predict the job stats {#ex-2.1}

Count from `rule all` backward. It asks for a FastQC report and a filtered BAM
for each of the ten samples:

| Rule | Jobs | Why |
|---|---:|---|
| `fastqc` | 10 | one per sample (`{sample}` in the output) |
| `filter` | 10 | one per sample |
| `align` | 10 | each `filter` job needs one aligned BAM |
| `bowtie2_index` | 1 | no wildcard: one job, shared by all ten `align` jobs |
| `all` | 1 | the target rule is a job too |
| **total** | **32** | |

The dry run agrees:

{{< generated name="stopA-dryrun" head="14" >}}

The rule that people miss is `all`. It runs no command, but Snakemake still
counts it as a job. The other thing to notice is that the table is sorted by
rule name, not by the order in which jobs run.

## Exercise 2.2: Make it ambiguous, then fix it {#ex-2.2}

The new rule's output, `{prefix}.bam.bai`, matches any file ending in
`.bam.bai`. `filter` also lists `{sample}_filtered.bam.bai` as an output. For
`output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam.bai` both rules fit, and
both have inputs Snakemake knows how to make:

<!-- GENERATE: stopA-ambiguous | stopping-points/stopA | cat >> Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule index_bam:
    input:
        "{prefix}.bam",
    output:
        "{prefix}.bam.bai",
    shell:
        "samtools index {input}"
EOF
snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam.bai || true -->

{{< generated name="stopA-ambiguous" command="false" >}}

The message is unusually helpful. It shows what each rule would set its
wildcards to (`prefix=output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered`: a wildcard
happily matches slashes) and suggests three fixes. The one asked for here is a
constraint, so `index_bam` only matches the BAMs nothing else indexes, the
aligned ones:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule index_bam:
    input:
        "{prefix}.bam",
    output:
        "{prefix}.bam.bai",
    wildcard_constraints:
        prefix = r".*_aligned",            # <1>
    shell:
        "samtools index {input}"
```

1. A regular expression the whole wildcard value must match. `.*_aligned`
   allows any path that ends in `_aligned`, so
   `output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered` no longer fits and only
   `filter` can make the filtered index.

<!-- GENERATE: stopA-ambiguous-fixed | stopping-points/stopA | cat >> Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule index_bam:
    input:
        "{prefix}.bam",
    output:
        "{prefix}.bam.bai",
    wildcard_constraints:
        prefix = r".*_aligned",
    shell:
        "samtools index {input}"
EOF
snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam.bai | awk '/^Job stats/ && !done {on=1} on {print} /^total/ && on {on=0; done=1}'
snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_aligned.bam.bai | awk '/^Job stats/ && !done {on=1} on {print} /^total/ && on {on=0; done=1}' -->

{{< generated name="stopA-ambiguous-fixed" command="false" >}}

The first table is for the filtered index (made by `filter`), the second for
the aligned index (made by `index_bam`).

A constraint inside a rule applies to that rule only. The block at the top of
stopping point B (`wildcard_constraints:` outside any rule) applies to every
rule. `ruleorder: filter > index_bam` would also work, but it hides the
overlap instead of removing it. Giving the general rule a narrower pattern
says what you meant.

## Exercise 2.3: Add samples {#ex-2.3}

After the first run with four CTCF samples (14 jobs: 4 each of `fastqc`,
`align` and `filter`, the index, and `all`), adding the two DNase samples
gives:

<!-- GENERATE: stopA-add-samples | stopping-points/stopA | sed -i -e '/"HCT116_H3K27ac_1", "HCT116_H3K27ac_2",/d' -e '/"HCT116_input-H3K27ac_1", "HCT116_input-H3K27ac_2",/d' -e '/"HCT116_DNase_1", "HCT116_DNase_2",/d' Snakefile
snakemake --cores 4 > /dev/null 2>&1
sed -i 's/^    "HCT116_input-CTCF_1", "HCT116_input-CTCF_2",/&\n    "HCT116_DNase_1", "HCT116_DNase_2",/' Snakefile
snakemake -n | awk '/^Job stats/ && !done {on=1} on {print} /^total/ && on {on=0; done=1}' -->

{{< generated name="stopA-add-samples" command="false" >}}

- Two of each per-sample rule, for the two new samples only. The CTCF
  outputs exist and are up to date, so they are not touched.
- No `bowtie2_index`: it exists and nothing it depends on changed.
- `all` runs again, because its input list grew.

This is what you want when a sequencing run comes back late: add the names
and run again, and only the new samples are processed. Module 3 makes it even
simpler, since you add a row to the samplesheet instead of editing code.

## Exercise 2.4: `{sample}` in the shell {#ex-2.4}

<!-- GENERATE: lesson02-shell-wildcard | stopping-points/stopA | cat > Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule fastqc:
    input:
        "../../data/fastq/{sample}.fastq.gz",
    output:
        html = "output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html",
        zip = "output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.zip",
    shell:
        "fastqc --outdir output/{sample}/fastqc {input}"
EOF
snakemake -n -p output/HCT116_CTCF_2/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_2_fastqc.html || true -->

{{< generated name="lesson02-shell-wildcard" command="false" >}}

The shell string is formatted with a fixed set of names (`input`, `output`,
`wildcards`, `params`, `threads`, `log`, `resources`, plus your global
variables). `sample` is not one of them, and Snakemake even suggests the
right spelling. With `-p` the dry run formats the command, so it catches the
mistake before anything runs. Without `-p`, you would only find out when the
job starts.

In `input:` and `output:` you write `{sample}`, because there it is a pattern.
In `shell:`, the value already exists and lives on the `wildcards` object.
